strengths: The core idea—clustering clients via loss vector embeddings rather than relying on models achieving lowest loss for cluster assignment—is a clean and well-motivated fix to the known initialization-sensitivity failure mode of IFCA, illustrated clearly and convincingly by the toy example in Figure 1.

The paper provides non-trivial theoretical analysis in a mixed linear regression setting, proving one-shot cluster recovery with high probability (via a proximity-condition argument building on Kumar-Kannan) and exponential convergence of per-cluster models across rounds, going beyond the purely empirical contributions of many CFL papers.

The empirical evaluation is broad: five datasets spanning image classification, text classification, and unsupervised image reconstruction, multiple heterogeneity types (label skew variants, feature skew, concept shift), comparison against 11 strong baselines (CFL, IFCA, FlexCFL, FeSEM, PACFL, FedProto, Per-FedAvg, FedALA, FedPAC), and convergence-speed and ARI metrics in addition to accuracy.

Useful ablations (matching strategy, clustering algorithm choice, square-root vs raw loss) and an explicit robustness-to-initialization experiment directly targeting the paper's central claimed advantage over IFCA.

The algorithm is simple to implement, generalizes FedAvg as a special case (K=1), and is one of few CFL methods explicitly shown to work in both supervised and unsupervised settings, which is a meaningfully broader scope than prototype- or gradient-based CFL methods that require labels.
weaknesses: The theoretical guarantees rely on a fairly narrow and stylized setting (isotropic Gaussian features, unit-norm well-separated optimal models, orthonormal or already-close-to-optimal model collections, small K relative to M and d, identical sample counts per cluster) that is far from the deep-network experiments in Section 5; the paper does not clearly bridge this gap or discuss how/whether the guarantees are expected to degrade for nonconvex, high-dimensional models.

Empirically, gains over the strongest baselines are often modest or inconsistent: e.g., CFL wins on CIFAR-10 concept-shift accuracy, FlexCFL wins on AG News, PACFL matches or beats CLoVE on some label-skew-4 ARI cases, and FedAvg wins Amazon Review accuracy outright, undercutting the abstract's claim of consistent state-of-the-art performance.

CLoVE requires broadcasting/evaluating all K models on every participating client each round (same as IFCA), which is not discussed as a scalability concern; for large K (many clusters) this multiplies both computation and communication, and the paper offers no scaling analysis or discussion of how performance/complexity changes as K grows.

Near-perfect (1.00 ± 0.00) ARI in the vast majority of Table 2/8 settings raises a question of whether the chosen skew intensities and per-client sample sizes (500 points) make clustering too easy to meaningfully differentiate strong methods; a systematic study of separation difficulty analogous to the linear-regression Δ sweep would strengthen the deep-learning claims.

Only 3 random seeds are used for all experiments, and no significance testing is reported beyond noting the ablation gap is meaningfully large; given the sometimes small performance deltas between top methods, this limits confidence in the significance of reported wins.

Privacy implications of sending per-model loss vectors to the server are dismissed in a single sentence without analysis (e.g., no discussion of potential membership-inference or gradient-leakage-adjacent risks), which is a somewhat cursory treatment of an ethically relevant aspect of the design.

Some recently cited related work (e.g., Kim et al. ICML'24 gradient-based partitioning, Werner et al. provably personalized/robust FL, Vardhan et al. improved federated clustering) is discussed but not empirically compared against, leaving open whether CLoVE's advantages hold against the most recent competitors.

strengths: The core idea—using per-client vectors of losses across all candidate models as an embedding for clustering—is simple, intuitive, and elegantly generalizes FedAvg (K=1) while avoiding IFCA's requirement that clients from the same cluster must already achieve lowest loss on the same model.

The paper provides a reasonably complete theoretical treatment for the mixed linear regression setting, including a one-shot cluster-recovery guarantee (Thm 4.1) and an exponential convergence guarantee (Thm 4.2), with an explicit comparison (Lemma A.17) showing IFCA's recovery condition implies CLoVE's but not vice versa.

The empirical evaluation is broad in scope: 5 datasets spanning image classification, text classification, and unsupervised image reconstruction, multiple heterogeneity regimes (label skew with and without overlap, feature skew, concept shift, dominant-class skew), and 10 competing baselines covering both CFL and generic PFL families.

Useful diagnostic analyses beyond raw accuracy: ARI-based cluster-recovery accuracy, convergence-speed tables (rounds to reach 90% ARI), an initialization-robustness study against IFCA, and ablations isolating the contribution of bipartite matching, clustering algorithm choice, and square-root loss transform.
The method is a lightweight, practical modification to standard clustered FL pipelines (only requires exchanging an additional K-length loss vector), making it easy to reproduce conceptually.
weaknesses: Significant theory-practice gap: the convergence/recovery guarantees are proven only for linear regression, and even there under an unusual configuration (N=d orthonormal models for the first round, then switching to K ∆-proximal models) that does not match the K-model procedure described in Algorithm 1 for the deep-learning experiments; the paper does not clearly bridge or acknowledge this mismatch, which undercuts the claim that theory explains the empirical deep-network results.

The empirical superiority of CLoVE is inconsistent and often marginal. In Table 1, several cells show CLoVE losing to FlexCFL, CFL, or FeSEM-type competitors by non-trivial margins (e.g., label skew 1 concept shift CIFAR-10, where CFL beats CLoVE); in Table 3, FedAvg and FlexCFL outperform CLoVE on Amazon Review and AG News respectively. The abstract's claim of "state-of-the-art accuracy" is not uniformly supported.

Clustering accuracy comparisons (Table 2, Table 8) frequently show multiple methods (FlexCFL, PACFL, CLoVE) tied at ARI=1.00, so CLoVE's claimed advantage in "highly accurate cluster recovery" is not clearly differentiated from several existing baselines in many settings; the advantage mainly appears in harder cases (feature/concept shift) but is not large enough or consistent enough to be convincing of a qualitative leap.

Statistical rigor is limited: only 3 random seeds are used, and several reported standard deviations are large relative to the mean differences between methods (e.g., Table 1 IFCA CIFAR-10 85.7±6.5, Table 4 IFCA/FlexCFL rows with huge variances), making many head-to-head claims of CLoVE's superiority statistically questionable without significance testing.

The most directly relevant recent CFL baseline addressing initialization sensitivity, [32] ("An Improved Federated Clustering Algorithm with Model-based Clustering"), is discussed in related work as addressing the same limitation as CLoVE but is never included as an empirical baseline, leaving the central claimed advantage (robustness to initialization) only validated against the older IFCA.

Important practical costs are not discussed or measured: CLoVE requires broadcasting and evaluating K full models per client per round (versus 1 for FedAvg), and the paper provides no communication/computation overhead analysis or scalability study for larger K (experiments cap at K≈10), which is a real concern for a method targeted at large numbers of real-world clusters.

The privacy discussion is dismissed in a single sentence claiming loss vectors reveal "nothing" beyond cluster membership, without any formal or empirical analysis (e.g., membership-inference or reconstruction risk from loss vectors), which is an unsupported claim given the paper markets CLoVE for "real-world applications."

Baseline fidelity is unclear: while GitHub links are provided for baseline implementations, there is no discussion of hyperparameter tuning effort applied equally to baselines versus CLoVE, raising concerns about comparison fairness, especially given how sensitive some PFL baselines (e.g., Per-FedAvg, FedALA) are known to be to tuning.

Presentation issues: the main paper relies heavily on forward references to a very long, dense appendix for all proofs and several key experiments (e.g., k-FED comparison, unsupervised scaling), making the paper's central empirical and theoretical claims hard to verify without extensive appendix cross-referencing; Figure 1's illustrative example, while helpful, is somewhat oversimplified relative to the complexity of the actual failure mode being described.

strengths: The core idea—clustering clients via loss vector embeddings rather than raw model selection—is simple, well-motivated, and clearly illustrated (Figure 1), addressing a genuine limitation of IFCA (sensitivity to initialization causing clients to collapse onto the same model).

The method applies naturally to both supervised and unsupervised settings since it only requires scalar loss values, which is a practical advantage over many CFL/PFL baselines that assume labeled data or gradient similarity.

Theoretical analysis for mixed linear regression is fairly detailed: it shows SLV means are separated for ortho-normal and Δ-proximal model collections, establishes one-shot cluster recovery via a proximity condition adapted from Kumar & Kannan, and shows exponential contraction of model error across rounds assuming correct matching.

The experimental evaluation is broad: 5 datasets (image, text, two task types), many types of heterogeneity (label skew variants, concept shift, feature skew), many baselines (11 total), and metrics beyond accuracy (ARI, convergence speed, robustness to initialization, ablations).
The robustness-to-initialization experiment and reconstruction-loss heatmap analysis (App. C.2.1) provide intuitive, convincing qualitative evidence for why CLoVE outperforms IFCA.
Ablation study isolates the contribution of bipartite matching, clustering algorithm choice, and square-root vs raw loss, lending some support to design choices.
Reasonably complete reproducibility details (architectures, hyperparameters, GitHub links for baselines, compute environment) are provided in the appendix.
weaknesses: Theoretical results are restricted to a fairly stylized mixed linear regression setting with strong assumptions (unit-norm optimal models, Δ close to 1, K small relative to M and d, balanced cluster sizes, ortho-normal or already Δ-proximal initializations); the leap to the nonlinear deep learning experiments in Section 5 is not theoretically justified, so the theory's relevance to the empirical results is limited.

The single-shot recovery theorem for the first round actually assumes ortho-normal model initialization, which does not correspond to standard random neural network initialization used in experiments—raising a gap between the theoretical guarantee (relies on specific structured initialization) and the empirical 'robustness to initialization' claims.

Empirical gains over the strongest baselines (e.g., CFL, FlexCFL, IFCA) are often modest and within or close to overlapping error bars in several table entries (e.g., Table 1 CIFAR-10 label skew 2, FMNIST concept shift), weakening the 'consistently state-of-the-art' claim; CLoVE is sometimes clearly outperformed (e.g., FlexCFL on AG News, FedAvg on Amazon Reviews).

The clustering overhead (broadcasting K models to each client and running all K forward passes per client per round) is not discussed in terms of added communication/computation cost relative to baselines that only maintain one assignment per client (e.g., IFCA also does this, but methods like gradient-based or prototype-based clustering may be cheaper); no wall-clock/communication cost comparison is given.
The claim that K (number of true clusters) is known a priori is a nontrivial assumption shared with several baselines but not critically discussed; sensitivity to misspecified K is not evaluated.
The paper's complexity analysis of the min-cost bipartite matching step and its scalability with increasing K is not discussed, which could be a practical bottleneck for larger numbers of clusters.

Statistical significance of results is only loosely addressed (3 seeds, standard deviations reported but no formal significance testing), making some comparative claims (e.g., 'CLoVE is the only algorithm that consistently ranks among top performers') somewhat overstated given the number of near-ties with baselines.

The privacy implications of sending per-model loss vectors to the server are dismissed briefly ('does not reveal anything about their data') without rigorous justification; loss values could still leak information (e.g., membership inference or data complexity signals) beyond cluster identity, which is a non-trivial claim to make without analysis.

strengths: The core idea—embedding clients via a full vector of losses across all cluster models rather than assigning to the single lowest-loss model (as in IFCA)—is simple, intuitive, and directly addresses a well-documented failure mode of IFCA (getting stuck when multiple clusters minimize loss on the same model due to poor initialization).

Theoretical analysis for the mixed linear regression setting is fairly thorough: it proves one-shot accurate cluster recovery with high probability (via a proximity condition adapted from Kumar & Kannan) without requiring the initial models to already be close to their optimal counterparts, and further proves exponential convergence of the learned models to the optimal ones. This addresses a real limitation of IFCA's theory.

Extensive empirical evaluation across many datasets (MNIST, CIFAR-10, FMNIST, FEMNIST, Amazon Reviews, AG News), tasks (image/text classification, unsupervised image reconstruction), skew types (label, feature, concept shift), and 11 baselines, with ablations, scaling experiments (up to 1000 clients), partial participation, unknown-K, and early-stopping studies—well beyond what is typical and quite convincing overall.
First extensive study of CFL in unsupervised settings, a relatively understudied area, showing consistent improvement over IFCA in reconstruction loss.

Good practical discussion of communication/computation overhead mitigation (early stopping upon cluster stability, layer sharing) and a candid discussion of privacy implications and limitations in the appendix.
Reasonable reproducibility support: hyperparameters, dataset partitioning procedures, and links to baseline implementations are given, and code availability is stated.
weaknesses: The theoretical guarantees only cover mixed linear regression with fairly strong assumptions (unit-norm optimal models, ∆ close to 1, very low noise σ≪1, ortho-normal or already-∆-proximal initial model collections, K known and small relative to M/d). This leaves a substantial gap to the neural-network experiments that constitute the paper's main empirical claims (e.g., robustness to arbitrary PyTorch default initialization is demonstrated only empirically, not theoretically).

Performance is not uniformly superior: in several settings (Amazon Reviews, AG News, Label skew 3, Label skew 4) other baselines like FedAvg, FlexCFL, or CFL-S outperform CLoVE, somewhat undercutting the "consistently top performer" framing; no statistical significance testing is reported despite reported standard deviations sometimes overlapping across methods.

CLoVE's overhead before stabilization (broadcasting and evaluating all K̂ candidate models each round, plus periodic silhouette-based search over candidate K) is nontrivial and not deeply compared quantitatively against baselines' costs (e.g., wall-clock or FLOPs), beyond a qualitative discussion in the appendix.

The core mechanism (deriving multi-model loss or gradient embeddings for clustering) is conceptually related to prior CFL work (e.g., CFL-S's gradient embeddings, FlexCFL), so the degree of novelty is somewhat incremental relative to those methods, even though the specific loss-vector formulation and theoretical treatment differ.

The silhouette-based selectBestK procedure and the assumption of near-orthonormal random initialization providing enough separation are not deeply justified for high-dimensional deep networks, where loss landscapes and initialization geometry differ substantially from the linear regression analysis.

The Impact Statement is minimal and does not meaningfully engage with potential societal implications (e.g., clustering could reveal sensitive latent group structure among clients), despite the paper's own privacy discussion in the appendix raising open questions.

strengths: The paper identifies a clear and intuitive failure mode of IFCA (initialization sensitivity causing collapse to fewer clusters than truly exist) and motivates the loss-vector-embedding idea well with a concrete illustrative example (Fig. 1).

Comprehensive empirical evaluation spanning six datasets, both supervised and unsupervised tasks, multiple types of heterogeneity (label skew, feature skew, concept shift), partial participation, unknown-K settings, and scaling experiments -- broader than most CFL papers, including a genuinely under-explored unsupervised CFL evaluation.

Provides a theoretical treatment (mixed linear regression) attempting to formally justify why loss-vector clustering can succeed even under low separability of raw data, with single-shot recovery and exponential convergence claims.

Numerous ablations (matching strategy, clustering algorithm, square-root vs. raw loss, FINCH vs k-means) and a discussion of communication/computation overhead and privacy considerations, showing awareness of practical deployment issues.
Practical mechanisms (early stopping/stability detection, handling unknown K via silhouette search) are described, which could reduce overhead relative to naive per-round full clustering.
weaknesses: Significant theory-practice gap: the theoretical guarantees require either d exactly orthonormal models or K models within ∆/4 of the true optima ('∆-proximal'), plus a low-noise/high-SNR regime and near-unit-norm, well-separated cluster centers. None of these conditions are verified or plausibly satisfied by PyTorch's default random initialization of neural networks used in the actual experiments, so the 'single-shot recovery with high probability' claim is not actually demonstrated for the settings studied empirically.

The core algorithmic novelty is incremental relative to IFCA (using the full vector of losses across K̂ models instead of the arg-min index) and is closely related to concurrent/cited work (FedGWC, gradient-based CFL); the paper's differentiation from FedGWC is argued informally in an appendix rather than empirically compared head-to-head in the main results tables.

Empirical superiority claims are overstated: CLoVE is not actually best in many settings (e.g., FedAvg wins on Amazon Reviews, FlexCFL wins on AG News and several ARI cases, IFCA/CFL-S occasionally match or exceed CLoVE), yet the text repeatedly asserts CLoVE 'consistently ranks among top performers' and achieves 'state-of-the-art' results, which overclaims relative to the mixed table results.

Several baselines display suspiciously poor and inconsistent performance (e.g., FeSEM at 11-15% accuracy on CIFAR-10 across many settings, near chance level), raising concerns about whether baselines were properly tuned/implemented, which undermines the credibility of the comparative claims.

Statistical rigor is limited: only 3 random seeds are used, and many reported accuracy/ARI differences have overlapping or comparable standard deviations, making some 'wins' for CLoVE not clearly statistically distinguishable from competitors.

Ablation results (e.g., agglomerative clustering slightly outperforming k-means, small effect of the matching step) suggest that several specific design choices touted as important in the main text are not strongly load-bearing, weakening the narrative that CLoVE's particular design choices are essential.

The privacy discussion is largely deferred/hand-wavy ('further research is needed'), and the paper does not empirically quantify the wall-clock/computation overhead of evaluating K̂ models per client each round, which is central to the claimed low-overhead advantage over baselines.

The main paper is extremely dense with an enormous appendix (35 pages) containing most of the substantive experimental detail and even key derivations, making the core contribution and its true scope difficult to assess from the main text alone.

strengths: The core idea—using vectors of per-client losses across multiple candidate models as an embedding for clustering—is simple, intuitive, and clearly motivated with an illustrative example (Fig. 1) contrasting it with IFCA's failure mode.

Rigorous theoretical analysis for the mixed linear regression setting: the paper proves that k-means on square-root loss vectors satisfies the (Kumar & Kannan, 2010) proximity condition for accurate one-shot cluster recovery, and separately proves exponential convergence of the per-cluster models to their optima. The proofs are detailed and internally consistent, with clearly articulated assumptions.

Very extensive empirical evaluation: six datasets, both supervised (image/text classification) and unsupervised (autoencoder reconstruction) tasks, multiple types of heterogeneity (label skew of several kinds, feature skew, concept shift), comparison against 10 baselines including recent CFL and generic PFL methods.

Numerous supporting studies beyond the main results: robustness to model initialization (vs. IFCA), unknown-K setting, early stopping/communication savings, partial participation (including the extreme case of fewer participants than clusters), scaling to up to 1000 clients, ablations on matching/clustering algorithm/loss transform, and comparison of model- vs. gradient-averaging variants.

The paper is the first (to the authors' knowledge) to provide an extensive evaluation of CFL in the unsupervised setting, an understudied but practically relevant scenario, and shows CLoVE's advantage there against IFCA.

Reasonably thorough discussion of communication/computation overheads and (qualitative) privacy considerations in the appendix, and honest acknowledgment that CLoVE's proof techniques leave certain generalizations (e.g., to plain loss vectors rather than square-root loss vectors, or tighter proximity bounds) for future work.
weaknesses: The theoretical guarantees are derived only for a restrictive mixed-linear-regression setting with several strong assumptions (near-unit-norm optimal models, K small relative to M and d, high SNR, i.i.d. Gaussian features), and it is unclear how much these guarantees say about the deep-learning settings used in the experiments; the connection between theory and practice is asserted rather than empirically validated in a matched setting.

The link(s) to the code repository appear to be left blank in the submitted PDF ("can be found here:" and "can be found at" with no URL), which currently limits verifiable reproducibility, even if this may be an anonymization artifact.

Performance gains over strong recent baselines (IFCA, FlexCFL, CFL-S) are sometimes modest or mixed (e.g., FlexCFL wins on AG News and some feature-skew ARI cases, FedAvg wins on Amazon Review, CFL-S occasionally leads test accuracy), so the claim that CLoVE is "state-of-the-art" across the board is only partially supported and could be tempered.

The method for determining the number of clusters when K is unknown (grid search over candidate K with silhouette score) adds computational overhead and is only lightly evaluated (a couple of datasets); its robustness in more complex, less well-separated real-world settings is not deeply explored.

The privacy discussion is qualitative and speculative ("further research is needed"); no formal privacy analysis or empirical leakage assessment (e.g., via membership-inference attacks) is provided despite loss vectors being additional information shared with the server compared to vanilla FedAvg.

Some baseline results exhibit very high variance (e.g., CFL-S ± 21.8 accuracy on MNIST), which makes some pairwise comparisons less statistically convincing, and only 3 random seeds are used throughout, which is a relatively small number for drawing strong statistical conclusions in noisy non-IID FL settings.
